title: Determ vs Awario vs Mention: Who Wins Brand Monitoring in 2026?
summary: Determ vs Awario vs Mention compared on pricing, ownership stability, and TikTok coverage — the gap all three budget monitoring tools still miss in 2026.
body_text: TL;DR: Determ, Awario, and Mention are the three budget-tier brand monitoring tools that keep showing up on the same shortlists — and each wins a different argument. Determ leads on traditional-media depth at a moderate price, Awario leads on affordability and a genuinely useful sales-intelligence feature, and Mention leads on raw platform count but became pricier and less independent after a 2025 acquisition by Agorapulse. None of the three actually analyzes TikTok video or audio content — the gap where consumer brands are losing the most signal in 2026. You've got three names on your shortlist, and they all look similar on paper. Determ, Awario, and Mention all promise to track your brand across the web, all publish (mostly) transparent pricing, and all show up in the same "best brand monitoring tools" roundups. Surface-level comparisons stop at "they all do keyword alerts." That's not enough to justify a year-long contract. What actually differs is who owns each company, what happened to Mention in the last two years, and whether any of them can see what's happening in a TikTok video rather than just its caption. This comparison is built for lean marketing and comms teams — beauty, F&B, fashion, consumer goods — who need a real verdict, not another feature grid. We'll walk through where each tool wins, what changed at Mention that most comparisons haven't caught up to yet, and the gap all three still share. Determ vs Awario vs Mention: At-a-Glance Comparison Determ is the PR-and-traditional-media specialist, Awario is the budget pick with a distinctive lead-generation angle, and Mention is the platform-count leader that recently changed hands. Here's how the three stack up on the criteria that actually matter for a purchase decision. Criteria Determ Awario Mention Starting Price €99/mo (Focus tier) $49/mo ($29/mo annual) $599/mo (Company Plan only) Top Published Tier €499/mo (Command) $399/mo ($249/mo annual) $599/mo (single tier) Pricing Model Monthly or annual, self-serve Monthly or annual, self-serve Annual billing only, no self-serve TikTok Coverage None None Caption/hashtag keyword matching only Traditional Media News, print, TV, radio (100M+ sources) Not surfaced in plan descriptions Not a stated strength Distinctive Feature Deep PR/news archive "Leads" sales-intelligence tool Broadest nominal platform list Ownership Independent since 2016 spinoff Bootstrapped, self-funded since 2015 Owned by Agorapulse since 2025 Public Rating 4.4/5 on Capterra (39 reviews) Not independently rated in this comparison G2 4.3/5 (442) · Capterra 4.7/5 (288) All three publish self-serve pricing, which already sets them apart from enterprise platforms like Brandwatch or Meltwater — but as the ownership row shows, "budget-friendly" and "stable" aren't the same thing (Source: Determ, 2026 ; Awario, 2026 ). How They Compare Head-to-Head Each tool was built to win a different job. Here's what each genuinely leads on — and where it falls short. Determ: Traditional Media and PR Depth Determ started as an in-house tool built by Croatian communications agency iStudio/Degordian, launched publicly in 2014 as Mediatoolkit, then spun off as an independent company in 2016. It rebranded to Determ in 2023 and still operates out of Zagreb without outside investors or an acquisition on its record — a track record Awario shares, and one Mention no longer can claim. That PR heritage shows in the product: Determ monitors over 100 million news sites plus print, TV, and radio alongside the usual social platforms (Facebook, Instagram, X, YouTube, Reddit, Bluesky, Medium, blogs, comments, forums). For a comms team tracking earned media alongside social chatter, that's a deep archive at a fraction of enterprise pricing. Where Determ wins: Traditional-media reach most budget tools skip entirely. A straightforward, published pricing ladder (€99–€499/mo). Independent ownership with a decade of continuity. Where it struggles: No TikTok coverage at any tier — Capterra reviewers flag this as a blind spot. Lower tiers cap history at 90 days, with occasional crashes noted too (Source: Capterra, 2026 ). Best for a PR or comms team that needs earned-media tracking alongside social and doesn't need TikTok. If Determ's ceiling is too low for your topic volume, see our Determ alternatives breakdown . Awario: The Budget Pick With a Sales Angle Awario is a bootstrapped sister product of Link-Assistant.Com (the company behind SEO PowerSuite), founded in 2015 by Aleh Barysevich and spun off as its own product in 2018. Like Determ, it's self-funded with no outside investors — a stability story that matters more given what happened at Mention. Awario's pricing is the most accessible of the three: $49/mo for 30,000 mentions, scaling to $399/mo for 1 million mentions plus API access. What sets it apart isn't just price — it's Leads, a feature that surfaces purchase-intent conversations rather than just brand mentions. Awario's own case study with agency client Upstack describes the feature as generating "millions in ARR" and having "more than paid for itself" within the first month (Source: Awario, 2026 ). Where Awario wins: The lowest entry price of the three with no compromise on core coverage breadth. Leads is a genuinely differentiated feature most competitors at this price point don't offer. Stable, independent ownership. Where it struggles: No TikTok-specific or video-analysis capability surfaced anywhere in its plans, and its traditional-media coverage documentation is thinner than Determ's. Best for a lean team that wants broad web/social coverage plus a sales-intelligence layer without enterprise pricing. Mention: Broadest Platform List, Now Under New Ownership Mention lists more platforms than either competitor on paper — TikTok, Instagram, Facebook, Pinterest, and YouTube alongside X, Reddit, web, news, blogs, forums, and 75+ review sites. But the mechanism matters: Mention's own copy describes monitoring "specific keywords used on the app... as real-time as the social network itself" — caption- and hashtag-level text matching, not analysis of what's actually said or shown in a video. The bigger story is what happened to Mention itself. Founded in Paris in 2012 by Arnaud Le Blanc, it was acquired by Mynewsdesk/NHST in 2018, then went through a French judicial bankruptcy recovery process around 2024, and was acquired out of that process by Agorapulse in March–April 2025. Reported deal values differ sharply by source — Dealroom cites €25M, while FrenchWeb's more granular reporting on the distressed-asset sale puts actual consideration closer to €4.67M, with only €61K distributed to creditors (Source: FrenchWeb, 2025 ; Dealroom, 2025 ). Mention now operates as "Mention by Agorapulse" — a product line, not an independent vendor. That acquisition already changed the product. In July 2025, Mention discontinued its self-serve tiers (Solo $49/mo, Pro $99/mo, Pro Plus $179/mo), replacing them with a single Company Plan at $599/month, annual billing only ($7,188/year), capped at 50,000 mentions across all alerts, with historical data and API access sold separately. As of January 30, 2026, its publishing and engagement features were retired outright, requiring a separate Agorapulse subscription (Source: Mention, 2026 ). Where Mention wins: The widest nominal platform list, including caption-level TikTok tracking the other two don't offer, plus strong review scores (G2 4.3/5, Capterra 4.7/5). Its own customer-story page (MyWHYagency, UFC-Que Choisir, WPX Hosting) is qualitative testimonial content, though — it doesn't publish the kind of quantified outcomes Awario's Leads case study does. Where it struggles: No self-serve entry point anymore — $599/mo, annual-only, is the floor, and product features are already being unbundled into a separate required subscription post-acquisition. Best for a team that specifically needs Mention's platform breadth and is comfortable with its new pricing floor and ownership structure. If that math doesn't work, see our Mention alternatives for video-first brands . Company Stability: Why Mention's Ownership Matters Vendor stability : how consistently a company's ownership, leadership, and core product commitments have held over time — a signal worth weighing alongside price and features, especially for a contract you intend to renew. Determ and Awario share something Mention no longer can: continuity, with neither ever going through a bankruptcy process or getting folded into a competitor's product line. Mention's January 2026 retirement of its publishing and engagement features — pushed into a separate required Agorapulse subscription — is a direct downstream effect of the 2025 acquisition, not an isolated decision. That doesn't make Mention a bad tool; it genuinely covers more platforms on paper than the other two. But a year-long contract is a bet on more than today's feature list, and Mention's is the only one of the three that comes with a recent ownership question mark attached. The Gap All Three Share: Native Video Analysis Here's what the Determ vs Awario vs Mention debate keeps missing. All three were built around keyword and Boolean matching — a model designed for a text-first internet of tweets, articles, and forum posts. Even Mention's "TikTok coverage," the broadest of the three, is really just caption and hashtag text matching applied to a video platform. Consumer conversations in beauty, F&B, and fashion have already moved past text. A beauty creator reviewing your product in a 45-second TikTok rarely types your brand name in the caption. A food creator recommending a snack in a Reel says it out loud. A fashion haul on YouTube Shorts shows the logo on camera without ever tagging it. Untagged mentions : brand conversations in video content where your brand is spoken aloud, shown visually, or referenced contextually — but never written in a caption, tag, or hashtag. Keyword-matching platforms structurally miss them, no matter how many platforms they claim to cover. None of the three can close that gap with more keyword rules, because the limitation isn't coverage breadth — it's the detection method. Syncly Social was built to close it: Audio Intelligence transcribes what creators actually say, and AI Vision reads on-screen text, logos, and visual context. See our social listening solution page for how that works alongside a budget monitoring tool rather than replacing it. How to Choose: Decision Framework Skip the feature grid. Match the tool to your actual workflow, then decide whether you need a video layer on top. If you run PR alongside social and need traditional-media depth → pick Determ. If budget is the top constraint and you want a sales-intelligence angle built in → pick Awario. If you specifically need Mention's platform breadth and are comfortable with $599/mo, annual-only pricing → pick Mention. If your audience lives on TikTok, Reels, and Shorts and you're missing what's actually said or shown on screen → add Syncly Social on top of whichever of the three you already use. If your team also needs to discover the creators already talking about your category → Creator Discovery surfaces them from the same content signal. None of these three tools requires a six-figure enterprise commitment, which is exactly why they end up on the same shortlist. The differentiator isn't price — it's what each one was built to see, and in Mention's case, who owns it now. Key Takeaways Determ wins on traditional-media depth — 100M+ news sources plus print, TV, and radio at €99–499/mo, with zero TikTok coverage at any tier Awario wins on affordability and its Leads feature — the lowest starting price ($49/mo) plus a sales-intelligence angle with a quantified case study Mention wins on nominal platform breadth but lost its independence — a 2025 acquisition by Agorapulse (following a 2024 bankruptcy recovery) eliminated its self-serve tiers and pushed pricing to $599/mo, annual-only Determ and Awario have stable, investor-free ownership histories; Mention's recent acquisition already triggered a January 2026 feature unbundling None of the three analyzes actual video or audio content — even Mention's TikTok coverage is caption/hashtag text matching, not speech or visual detection Conclusion Determ, Awario, and Mention are all legitimate answers — to different questions. Determ is the traditional-media specialist. Awario is the budget-and-sales-intelligence pick. Mention is the platform-count leader, now operating under new ownership with a much higher price floor than it had a year ago. Picking between them on price or feature count alone misses the bigger question: which one matches how your team works, and how much stability you need from a year-long vendor relationship. Either way, all three are still reading captions and hashtags in a world where your customers increasingly just talk on camera — for B2C brands where TikTok, Reels, and Shorts are the primary channel, that's the gap worth closing next. title: Looker Pricing: Is It Worth It In 2026? [Reviewed]
summary: I’ll go over Looker’s pricing to help you make an informed decision.
body_text: Looker pricing has a page on Google Cloud that never names a price for the platform itself. Three editions and three seat types, with the same two words next to every one of them: call sales. So I went past the pricing page. I read what Google's own documentation says about editions and trials, then collected the figures that procurement sites and rival BI vendors report, and went back to each original source to see whether it still held up. Several didn't, and I'll show you which ones. ➡️ There's a Looker alternative I'll come to later: Dot, an AI analyst that does the digging itself and delivers written findings into Slack or Teams, with no LookML model required to get started. TL;DR Looker bills on two meters: a platform fee for running the instance, and a separate license for every user on it, both quoted by sales on an annual commitment of one, two, or three years. There's no free plan, though Google does offer 90-day trial instances of all three editions. The only dollar figures Google publishes for Looker itself are the Conversational Analytics overage rates, at $3.00 per 1M input data tokens and $20.00 per 1M output data tokens, with billing starting October 1, 2026. For teams whose data already reaches a warehouse, Dot is the one alternative I'd weigh: our decision intelligence software does the analysis and hands back written findings in Slack or Teams, and it maintains the metric layer itself, with an admin approving any change. How Does Looker Calculate Its Pricing? Looker’s pricing is calculated with 2 factors: Platform pricing covers running the Looker instance itself, including the semantic modeling layer and platform administration. User pricing is the license attached to each person who logs in, and it changes with what that person is allowed to do. Source of image. Every instance you create has a Google Cloud billing account attached to it, and new instances and new named users both land on that account. Four things will shape your budget more than the edition you choose: The platform fee is a floor: Each edition includes ten Standard Users and two Developer Users. The edition locks at creation: Google's documentation is direct about it, so moving up later means a new instance and a data import. API ceilings arrive with the edition: Standard allows 1,000 query-related and 1,000 admin-related calls a month, Enterprise 100,000 and 10,000, Embed 500,000 and 100,000. The Power BI and Tableau connectors draw on that budget, as does Looker's MCP server, and API access is Developer-only. Staging bills like production: Non-production instances are bought separately at the same rate, and Google advises Embed buyers to budget for one. ➡️ Note: Looker is the enterprise platform Google Cloud sales quotes you, LookML and embedding included, on an annual commitment. Looker Studio is a different product with a free tier and a paid Pro option. Don't price one from the other. Does Looker Have a Free Plan or Free Trial? Looker does not offer a free plan, and every paid edition is an annual contract priced by sales. However, there’s a free trial that you can sign up for. Source of image. Google's documentation confirms you can create a trial instance of Standard, Enterprise, or Embed, with the same feature support as the matching production edition. The limits are real, though: Trial instances run for 90 days, after which you delete or upgrade. There's no direct upgrade path, so going paid means creating a new instance and importing your trial data into it. You get one active trial per edition type for each combination of Google Cloud project and region. Data Studio Pro licenses aren't included with a trial, or with any Looker instance created after August 1, 2026. Source of image. Looker's Plan Breakdowns Three platform editions, all annual, all quoted by sales. Standard edition Built for teams under 50 internal platform users. Source of image. You get: One production instance, with ten Standard Users and two Developer Users. Google Cloud IAM access management and simplified BigQuery connectivity. Up to 1,000 query-related and 1,000 admin-related API calls a month. Platform upgrades. Enterprise edition Everything in Standard, with the user cap lifted and the security controls added. Source of image. On top of Standard: Unlimited platform users, though every one of them still needs a paid license. More security features, such as VPC-SC, Private connections (Private Service Connect), and Private connections (private services access). A private label option, FIPS encryption, and compliance certifications. Up to 100,000 query-related and 10,000 admin-related API calls a month. Deployments of any real size tend to end up on Enterprise, usually once the Standard cap and the API allowance run out together. Embed edition Everything in Enterprise, pointed at analytics inside a product your own customers use. Source of image. What it adds: Signed embedding, which no other edition includes. Impersonation of embed users through the Login user API endpoint. Up to 500,000 query-related API calls a month. Up to 100,000 admin-related API calls a month. What are Looker's user licenses? Seat cost tracks permission. The three tiers divide up like this: License Can do Can't do Developer User Everything a Standard User can do, plus administration, LookML development in Development Mode, the Looker API, and support access Nothing listed Standard User Folders, boards, dashboards, Looks, Explore, SQL Runner, scheduling, dashboard and Look creation, filtering, drill to row-level detail, downloads, view-only LookML Development Mode, administration, the API, support Viewer User Folders, boards, dashboards, Looks, filtering, drill to row-level detail, scheduling, downloads, view-only LookML Dashboard and Look creation, Explore, SQL Runner, Development Mode, administration, the API, support Source of image. Google also reserves the right to invoice in arrears if your usage runs past what your subscription covers. Conversational Analytics data tokens This is the one place Google prints real numbers. Gemini-powered Conversational Analytics is metered in data tokens, pooled at the instance level across every authenticated user on it. Input tokens cover the prompt and everything sent alongside it, including session history and context. Output tokens cover the written reply, the generated SQL, reasoning shown in Thinking mode, and any visualization the model builds. Each subscription carries a monthly allowance: Platform tier Included input tokens Included output tokens Standard 60M 1.2M Enterprise 300M 6M Embed 1.2B 24M Source of image. Non-production and add-on instances get a flat 6M input and 0.12M output tokens a month. Allowances reset monthly, and nothing rolls over. What Do Third-Party Sources Report Looker Costs? ⚠️ Disclaimer: everything in this section comes from third parties, none of it from Google. We haven't independently verified any of it, some of it traces back to pages that have since changed or vanished, and none of it is a list price, so treat these as estimates and get a quote. With that said, these are the figures in circulation: The most-quoted Looker numbers on the internet come from an old AWS Marketplace retail listing: $66,600 a year for the Standard platform, $132,000 for Advanced, and $198,000 for Elite, with add-on seats at $400 for a Viewer, $799 for a Standard User, and $1,665 for a Developer. Those tier names line up with Google's current editions, and Google's own token table confirms the mapping by carrying the Advanced and Elite labels alongside Enterprise and Embed. The catch is that Looker's AWS Marketplace listings have been withdrawn and now read as removed and unavailable to new customers. So these are historical list prices that keep getting recirculated as current ones. Vendr's Looker (old?) buyer guide is where the widely repeated "$150,000 average, $1,770,000 maximum, 355 deals" figures came from publishers like Holistics . Those numbers are no longer displayed on the page, and the panel where average contract value used to appear is now blank. Community posts like this one put $60,000 a year for the Standard edition. Business reviews that arrive already written Dot generates recurring business reviews on the cadence you set, querying live warehouse data and delivering an executive-ready report to Slack or email with the period-over-period numbers and a written read on what moved. With Dot, you set the schedule and the source once, and the finished review arrives every cycle. title: RFP Examples: 7 Real Structures, Industry Samples, and How to Read One
summary: See what real RFPs look like section by section, with RFP examples across seven industries, a sample outline to adapt, and reading tips for vendor teams.
body_text: Most people searching for RFP examples want the same thing: to see a real one before they write one, or before they answer one. The second group is larger than most example roundups acknowledge. For every procurement manager drafting a request for proposal , there are a dozen vendor teams on the receiving end working to understand it, judge their chances, and decide whether the next 30 hours of response work is worth it. This guide serves both readers. It covers the anatomy of a standard RFP, a sample outline you can adapt, examples of what RFPs look like across seven US industries, and one thing most examples posts leave out: how to read an RFP the way experienced proposal teams do, so the document tells you whether to bid before you write a word. Key Takeaways An RFP is the document a buyer issues when the purchasing decision depends on capability and fit, not price alone. It differs from an RFQ (a price on a fixed spec) and an RFI (early market research) . Nearly every RFP shares seven sections: cover page, background, scope of work, submission requirements, evaluation criteria, pricing instructions, and terms and conditions. The structure holds across industries, but the emphasis shifts. Software RFPs are requirement-heavy, healthcare RFPs are compliance-gated, and consulting RFPs focus on named individuals. Before responding, spend twenty minutes reading the RFP for its evaluation weights, mandatory pass/fail gates, timeline fairness, and any deal-breaking terms. The best RFPs publish their scoring weights, write an unambiguous scope, and consolidate their Q&A. Each is a signal vendors can use to judge how mature and winnable an opportunity is. What Is an RFP? A Sixty-Second Refresher A request for proposal (RFP) is a formal document a buyer issues to solicit detailed proposals from vendors when the purchasing decision depends on more than price. The buyer describes a problem, sets requirements, and asks vendors to respond with an approach, a team, a timeline, and a cost. Those proposals are then scored against published or unpublished criteria, and a winner is selected. An RFP is one of three related documents that buyers often confuse : Document What the buyer wants When it gets issued RFP (Request for Proposal) A full proposal: approach, methodology, team, pricing The decision rests on capability and fit alongside cost RFQ (Request for Quotation) A price on a fixed, clearly defined spec The spec is locked and price is the deciding variable RFI (Request for Information) Market intelligence, capability overviews The buyer is still scoping the category or building a shortlist For vendors who respond to RFPs regularly, the difference between these documents is practical, not academic. An RFQ rewards the sharpest price on a fixed spec. An RFP rewards a response that mirrors the buyer's evaluation structure. Treat the two the same way, and you will lose both. Also Read: Your Ultimate Guide to RFPs (Request for Proposals) RFP Structure: The 7 RFP Sections in Nearly Every Example Read enough RFPs and a clear pattern emerges. Whether the issuer is a county government, a hospital system, or a SaaS company sourcing a new vendor, the same seven sections appear in some order. Here is what each one does, and what a vendor should look for inside it. 1. Cover page and administrative summary This section lists the RFP title, reference number, issuing organization, issue date, and submission deadline. It looks routine, but it is also the first place deals are lost. Vendor teams that skim past the reference number or the required submission method get disqualified on technicalities that have nothing to do with the quality of their solution. 2. Background and statement of need This section explains who the buyer is and why they are going to market now. Strong examples keep it to a few paragraphs. For vendors, it is where you find the real problem behind the procurement, which is rarely stated as directly anywhere else in the document. 3. Scope of work The scope of work is the heart of the RFP: deliverables, timelines, volumes, service levels, what is included, and what is explicitly excluded. A vague scope produces proposals that cannot be compared against one another. If you are responding and the scope can be read three different ways, submit clarifying questions early. Guessing at scope is how a bid priced for 200 users loses to one priced for 2,000, or the reverse. 4. Submission requirements and timeline This section covers format, page limits, required forms, the question-and-answer window, and the full procurement calendar from issue date to award. Federal and state response windows in the US commonly run 30 to 60 days, while commercial RFPs often allow two to four weeks. 5. Evaluation criteria This section explains how proposals will be scored. The best examples publish the weights outright, for example technical approach 30%, pricing 25%, team and references 20%, implementation plan 15%, and compliance 10%. When the weights are published, your response outline should follow them almost mechanically. We break down real scoring frameworks in our guide to RFP evaluation criteria examples . 6. Budget and pricing instructions Some issuers disclose a budget range or ceiling. Most provide a pricing template instead and ask for a specific cost breakdown. Follow the template exactly, because pricing presented in your own format reads as evasive. 7. Terms and conditions This section covers contract terms, insurance minimums, confidentiality, payment terms, and compliance standards. Vendors should read it before writing anything else. A net-90 payment term or an uncapped liability clause you cannot accept is a reason to walk away on day one, not a surprise to discover in week three. Knowing the seven sections is step one. Inventive's AI agents read every one and draft a complete, source-cited response from your own approved content — your team just reviews and sends. Book a demo → A Sample RFP Template Outline You Can Adapt A Sample RFP Template Outline You Can Adapt Here is an example that reflects how well-constructed US RFPs are organized. Issuers can copy it and fill it in. Vendors can use it as a checklist for what a complete RFP should include, and for what to ask about when something is missing. REQUEST FOR PROPOSAL Issued by: [Organization] RFP Title: [Category or project name] Reference No: [Number] | Issue Date: [Date] Questions Due: [Date] | Proposals Due: [Date, time, time zone] 1. BACKGROUND AND PURPOSE Who we are, the problem we are solving, why now, and approximate scale or contract value if disclosable. 2. SCOPE OF WORK Deliverables, timelines, volumes, SLAs. In scope. Explicitly out of scope. 3. SUBMISSION REQUIREMENTS Response format and method. Page limit. Pricing template. Late submissions policy. Pre-proposal conference details, if any. 4. TIMELINE Issue date, Q&A window, answers published, proposals due, evaluation period, award date. 5. EVALUATION CRITERIA Published scoring weights by category. Any mandatory pass/fail requirements. 6. VENDOR QUESTIONNAIRE Structured questions, each mapped to a criterion. 7. TERMS AND CONDITIONS Contract terms, insurance, confidentiality, compliance. 8. APPENDICES Required forms, pricing sheets, technical specs. RFP Examples by Industry: 7 Real Sample RFPs The seven-section example holds across industries, but the emphasis shifts from one sector to the next. Here is what RFPs actually look like in seven US sectors, and what vendor teams should notice in each. Technology and software RFPs Software RFPs contain a high volume of detailed requirements. Expect functional requirement matrices, integration requirements, data migration questions, security questionnaires attached as appendices, and user counts that drive pricing. Real documents you can open right now: City of Duluth, MN: case management software RFP . A municipal software procurement with required forms and both paper and digital submission, typical of how local governments buy systems. Institute of International Education: web design and hosting services RFP . Issued in 2026 with a five-year performance period, it shows how a long-term service relationship gets scoped and priced. COAST transit authority (NH): website redesign and maintenance RFP . A compact 2026 example of a small public agency structuring a web project without overcomplicating it. Vendor takeaway: the security and compliance sections are usually pass/fail gates. Answer them completely and literally. A vague line such as "we take security seriously" reads as a non-answer and can get you disqualified. Marketing and creative services RFPs Marketing and creative RFPs combine a defined structure with room for the agency's creative judgment. The strongest ones hand agencies the raw materials, brand guidelines, audience data, and campaign objectives, then evaluate responses on strategic thinking and past campaign results rather than feature checklists. Two worth studying: Monterey County CVB: agency of record RFP . It provides rich background on the destination's business plan, target market, and team structure, exactly the raw material an agency needs to respond well. Silicon Valley Clean Energy: marketing and advertising services RFP . A clear multi-channel scope from a public agency, with submission requirements agencies can follow without guesswork. Vendor takeaway: in practice, marketing and creative buyers often give heavy weight to team rapport and portfolio strength, even when the published criteria emphasize other factors. Named team members and relevant case work carry the response. Construction RFPs In construction RFPs, the scope of work section is often longer and more decisive than the rest of the document combined. Expect bills of quantities, technical drawings attached as appendices, prequalification gates, milestone payment structures, and non-negotiable safety standards. Real documents to study: NYC Health + Hospitals: construction management services RFP . A 2026 solicitation from one of the largest US public health systems, seeking up to seven construction management firms for as-needed infrastructure and modernization work. Hesperia Recreation and Park District: public works construction RFP . A 2026 posting covering facility restoration, roofing, HVAC, electrical, and plumbing across multiple sites. Incourage Community Foundation: construction manager RFP . Seven pages, with the issuer's vendor priorities stated on page one, proof that a good RFP does not need to be long. Vendor takeaway: prequalification requirements come first. If you cannot clear them, the quality of the rest of your proposal will not matter. Our construction RFP template shows the full structure. Healthcare RFPs In healthcare RFPs, compliance is a pass/fail gate rather than a scored criterion, which means it can eliminate you before your proposal is ever evaluated. HIPAA obligations, data residency, and interoperability requirements sit at the front of hospital and payer RFPs, and vendors who cannot attest to them are removed before scoring begins. Open these: Puerto Rico Health Insurance Administration: State Funded Health Plan RFP . A 2026 payer-side procurement soliciting managed care organizations, dense with the compliance and reporting requirements that define healthcare RFPs. University of New Mexico Hospital: strategic healthcare consultant RFP . Note how the evaluation criteria weight technical approach, management approach, experience, and cost, a common pattern for consulting engagements. Vendor takeaway: generic security language reads as a red flag to healthcare evaluators. Cite the specific certification, the audit date, and the scope it covers. Financial services RFPs Asset management, banking, and insurance RFPs are among the longest and most standardized you will encounter. Expect tables for assets under management, client base reporting, fee structure disclosures, and lengthy qualification sections. Two real examples: Office of the State Treasurer of Delaware: endowment manager RFP . It includes the assets-under-management and client-base reporting tables that define this category. Town of Cutler Bay, FL: financial advisory services RFP . A compact 2026 municipal example showing the same qualification-heavy structure at smaller scale. Vendor takeaway: these issuers compare responses cell by cell, so precision and completeness matter more than narrative, the opposite of the marketing RFP above. Reading the document type correctly is half the response strategy. Professional services and consulting RFPs In consulting RFPs, the buyer is hiring the specific people who will do the work, not the firm's brand. These RFPs ask for named team members, individual CVs, time commitments, and a plan for what happens when a key person leaves mid-engagement. Real documents to study: Morrow County, OR: project management services RFP . It states three pass/fail criteria in plain language, on-time submission, proposal completeness, and copy count, small details that disqualify real vendors. New Jersey City University: data analytics consultant RFP . A thorough question list plus a supplier diversity policy, showing how universities structure consulting procurements. Vendor takeaway: answer the key-person question honestly and specifically. Evaluators use it to tell firms with real staffing depth from firms that only look strong on paper. See our consulting RFP template for the standard structure. Government RFPs Federal solicitations follow the Uniform Contract Format, a thirteen-section structure (Sections A through M) defined in the Federal Acquisition Regulation. Section C holds the statement of work, Section L tells you exactly what to submit, and Section M tells you exactly how it will be scored. FAR 15.203 requires solicitations to disclose evaluation factors and their relative importance. State and local RFPs are less rigid but follow a recognizably similar logic. To read live federal RFPs in full, browse SAM.gov's contract opportunities , the government's official portal for open solicitations. For how public-sector issuers think about structuring these documents, the Harvard Government Performance Lab's RFP guidebook is a strong, permanent public reference. Vendor takeaway: experienced government proposal teams read Section L first, Section M second, and Section C third. Compliance with Section L and alignment to Section M decide awards more often than the quality of the writing does. Every RFP starts the same way: digging each question out of a dense document. Inventive AI extracts them all in minutes — PDF, Word, Excel, or PowerPoint. Book a demo → How Vendors Should Read an RFP Before Writing a Word RFPs decide how enormous sums are spent. In fiscal year 2024, the U.S. federal government alone obligated about $755 billion through contracts, much of it via competitive solicitations, according to the U.S. Government Accountability Office . A single response can absorb dozens of hours, and you win only a share of what you bid, so before committing that time, spend the first twenty minutes on a structured read: Find the evaluation weights. If technical approach carries 30% and price carries 25%, concentrate your best material in that same proportion. If no weights are published, treat that as information too: it often signals a less mature procurement, or one where the buyer already has a preferred vendor in mind. List every mandatory requirement and pass/fail gate. Certifications, insurance minimums, reference counts, and submission formats are each binary. Miss one and the other 114 answers never get read. Check the timeline for fairness. A complex RFP issued on a Monday with a deadline that Friday usually means an incumbent is already favored and the process is largely a formality. You can still bid if the relationship is worth building, but do it knowing the odds. Read the terms before the questionnaire. Deal-breaking payment or liability terms surface within minutes and can save you the entire response effort. Run a real go/no-go decision. Weigh strategic fit, competitive position, resource cost, and win probability. Teams that skip this step respond to everything and win less. The RFP questions vendors should ask before committing are worth building into a standing checklist. RFP Best Practices: What Strong Examples Do Differently Every example above, from the county construction RFP to the federal solicitation, is ultimately judged by the proposals it produces. These six practices separate RFPs that attract strong, comparable proposals from those that produce weak or mismatched ones, and each carries a lesson for the vendors responding, too. 1. Publish the evaluation weights Some buyers hide their scoring weights, assuming disclosure gives away their strategy. In practice, publishing the weights helps them: vendors who know that implementation carries 15% write focused implementation sections instead of guessing. For vendors: when weights are published, mirror them in your structure. Evaluators score responses organized around their own criteria more easily, and they notice when you have done it. 2. Write a scope that can only be read one way Specify volumes, user counts, locations, and boundaries. An ambiguous scope produces bids ranging from $50K to $500K for the same work, none of which can be compared. For vendors: ambiguity is your cue to use the Q&A window actively. Every clarifying question you ask is answered for all bidders, which levels the field and sharpens your own estimate. 3. Keep the questionnaire tied to scoring Twenty questions, each mapped to an evaluation criterion, beat forty-five questions that serve curiosity rather than scoring. Vendors juggling eight RFPs a month will deprioritize the bloated one. For vendors: when you do face a 100-question RFP, answer placement matters. Put the substance in the answer itself rather than pointing evaluators to an appendix they are unlikely to open. 4. Give vendors enough time to be thoughtful Two weeks is the floor for commercial RFPs of any complexity, and public-sector windows of 30 to 60 days exist for a reason: response quality drops sharply when timelines compress. For vendors: treat a short window as a factor to weigh in your go/no-go decision, not just a frustration. Teams with automated first drafts can handle compressed timelines that manual teams cannot. 5. Put deal-breaker terms in plain sight Net-90 payment, uncapped liability, and mandatory on-site presence are all terms that can end a deal. Burying them in an appendix wastes three weeks of everyone's evaluation effort. For vendors: look for these terms in your first read, precisely because many issuers do bury them. 6. Consolidate and publish the Q&A Answering each vendor privately creates unequal information and duplicate work, while a single published Q&A document keeps the process clean. For vendors: read the full consolidated Q&A even for questions you did not ask. Competitor questions reveal how the field is interpreting the scope, and sometimes reveal who your competitors are. Answers drawn from knowledge you already have. The Knowledge Hub connects to SharePoint , Google Drive , Salesforce , Confluence , Notion , and more, so there is no new content repository to build or maintain. Drafts with citations and confidence scores. Every generated answer shows its source, and when the information does not exist, the agent flags it as unavailable instead of guessing. A Content Governance Agent that keeps knowledge current. Conflicting, outdated, and duplicate content is flagged automatically, so the answer library stays trustworthy between RFPs. Strategic agents for the hard parts. A Go/No-Go Agent scores the opportunity early, and a Full Response Analyzer checks the finished response for compliance gaps and contradictions before submission. Insider cut RFP response time by 90% and lifted win rate from 30% to 50%. See it work through one of your own RFPs. Book a demo → Also Read: Best AI RFP Software 2026: Ranked & Compared Frequently Asked Questions How many questions does a typical RFP include? There is no standard length. Commercial software RFPs range from a few dozen questions to well over a hundred, while government solicitations often pair a shorter questionnaire with heavy compliance documentation. Size your response effort to the questionnaire in front of you, not to any industry average. How long do vendors usually get to respond to an RFP? Vendors usually get 30 to 60 days to respond to US public-sector RFPs, with complex procurements allowing 90 days or more. Commercial RFPs move faster, often two to four weeks. Anything under two weeks for complex work is a signal worth weighing in your go/no-go decision. What should a vendor do when an RFP is vague or missing details? When an RFP is vague, use the question period, and use it early. Submit specific clarifying questions about scope boundaries, volumes, and evaluation weights. Answers are typically published to all bidders, so asking costs you no competitive ground. If the issuer declines to clarify anything material, document your assumptions explicitly in the proposal. What are pass/fail criteria in an RFP? Pass/fail criteria are requirements evaluated as binary gates before scoring begins, such as mandatory certifications, insurance minimums, on-time submission, required reference counts, or specific compliance attestations. A proposal that misses even one is typically eliminated regardless of how well it scores elsewhere, which is why experienced teams extract every mandatory requirement into a checklist before drafting. Do government RFPs follow a standard format? Federal government RFPs follow the Uniform Contract Format, thirteen sections labeled A through M, with proposal instructions in Section L and evaluation factors in Section M. State and local formats vary by jurisdiction but usually mirror the same logic: scope, submission rules, evaluation criteria, and terms in a predictable order. Should an RFP disclose the budget? Practice is split on whether an RFP should disclose the budget. Disclosing a range or ceiling produces proposals scoped to reality and saves both sides from a $50K-versus-$500K spread. Issuers who withhold the budget usually do so to avoid anchoring prices. For vendors, an undisclosed budget makes the Q&A window and your own discovery questions more important, not less. ‍

title: Agent Assist vs. AI Agent: What's the Real Difference?
summary: Agent assist vs AI agent: understand the real difference, when each approach fits, and how to choose the right model for your contact center in 2025.
body_text: Picture a health insurance call center on a Monday morning. Fifty agents are logged in, each fielding back-to-back calls about plan renewals, billing disputes, and prior authorization questions. On one screen, every agent has a sidebar panel that listens to the live call and surfaces suggested responses, relevant policy snippets, and compliance prompts in real time. On another screen, a completely separate set of phone lines is being handled without any human agent involved at all. A voice speaks, gathers member information, verifies identity, checks eligibility, and either resolves the issue or routes the caller to a specialist with a full summary already attached. Both of those systems use artificial intelligence. Both handle phone calls. But they are not the same thing, and choosing the wrong one for the wrong job creates expensive, visible problems. The confusion between agent assist and AI agent is not just a terminology problem. It shapes purchasing decisions, staffing models, compliance architecture, and the experience millions of callers have every day. In 2025, as contact center AI investment accelerates, that confusion has real consequences. This post breaks down the actual difference between agent assist and AI agent technology, where each genuinely excels, and where each one falls short. If you are an operations or revenue leader at a financial services firm, a healthcare organization, or an insurance carrier trying to decide where to place your next technology bet, this is the distinction you need to get right. The Agent Assist Definition: A Copilot, Not a Pilot Agent assist (sometimes written as AI agent assist) is a category of software that runs alongside a human agent during a live interaction. It does not take the call. It does not speak to the customer. Instead, it listens, analyzes, and advises the human who is doing the talking. A practical agent assist definition: software that uses AI to give human agents real-time recommendations, information retrieval, and compliance guidance during a live customer interaction, without replacing the agent in the conversation. Typical agent assist capabilities include: Real-time transcription of the conversation as it happens Suggested responses or next-best-action prompts based on what the customer just said Knowledge base retrieval that surfaces relevant articles, scripts, or policy language Compliance alerting , such as flagging when an agent is about to say something that violates a regulatory disclosure requirement Sentiment detection , helping supervisors spot a call going sideways before it escalates Automatic after-call work , such as pre-filling call notes and CRM updates based on the transcript Agent assist has been one of the fastest-growing categories in contact center software because it offers a relatively low-risk entry point into AI. You keep your existing agents, you keep your existing workflows, and you layer intelligence on top. According to contact centers deploying agent assist tools have reported meaningful reductions in average handle time and improvement in first-call resolution rates. The appeal is obvious: no rip-and-replace of your staffing model, a shorter change-management cycle, and a human always in the loop. The AI Agent Definition: A Pilot, Not a Copilot An AI agent is a system that handles a customer interaction autonomously, from beginning to end or through a defined portion of the conversation, without a human agent in the loop unless a handoff is explicitly triggered. In a voice context, an AI voice agent answers the phone, speaks with the caller using natural language, retrieves data, executes actions (such as booking an appointment or updating an account record), and either resolves the interaction completely or transfers the caller to a human with full context attached. The AI agent is the agent for that interaction. There is no human listening behind the glass. This distinction matters in several important ways: Scale. An AI agent can handle hundreds or thousands of simultaneous calls. An agent assist tool is still bounded by the number of human agents you have. Cost structure. AI agents change the unit economics of a call center fundamentally. Agent assist reduces the cost-per-call at the margin. AI agents can eliminate a category of call volume from human staffing entirely. Ownership of outcomes. With agent assist, the human agent is still accountable for the conversation. With an AI agent, the system itself is accountable, which means your AI platform's compliance posture, accuracy, and escalation logic matter enormously. Deployment complexity. Agent assist is typically layered onto an existing contact center platform. AI agents often require integration with your telephony stack, your CRM, your knowledge base, and your escalation routing, either through a developer build or a vendor platform like Feather AI that bundles all of those layers together. The line between these two categories has blurred as vendors have pushed into adjacent territory. Some agent assist tools now claim to handle simple intents autonomously. Some AI agent platforms offer human-in-the-loop review modes. But the architectural distinction, and the operational implications, remain fundamentally different. Why This Confusion Is Costing Businesses Real Money The agent assist vs. AI agent confusion surfaces most sharply in two failure modes. Failure mode one: Buying agent assist when you actually need AI agents. A financial services company has 400 inbound calls per day for routine account balance inquiries and payment confirmations. They deploy an agent assist tool and see modest improvements in handle time. But they still need 20 agents taking those 400 calls. The AI is helping those agents go slightly faster, but it is not changing the fundamental staffing equation. They have spent significant budget on a tool that did not address their actual problem, which was call volume that outpaced headcount. Failure mode two: Deploying AI agents without understanding the compliance implications. A healthcare organization deploys an AI agent to handle appointment scheduling calls. No one has validated whether the system is HIPAA-compliant. No one has reviewed whether the escalation logic meets the organization's clinical triage standards. The AI agent handles calls, but it creates new legal and reputational risk because the compliance architecture was treated as an afterthought. Getting this distinction right is not academic. It is the difference between a technology investment that solves a business problem and one that creates new ones.

title: 🐝 Efficient Tokens & Effective Teams in Buzz
summary: How do you migrate 2000+ apps without losing your mind? You build an AI Swarm. Advice and benchmarks for Buzz!
body_text: Buzz agents get their own persona, memory, and its own seat in the channel, so a group of them can chase one goal together with you in the room. Once spinning up a team is that easy, the questions are: How do I build the right team? What is the cheapest team that can reliably succeed? So we ran some targeted benchmarks with real Buzz agents on a live relay. The agents pick up the task as an ordinary Buzz message on the relay and reply as they work with each other. None of the results below were measured on a stripped-down test rig. What follows is the latest advice, and the benchmark numbers that earned it. TL;DR - Right bee. Right team. Right task. 🐝 Hives and Swarms: Keep Hives that learn how you work. Build temporary Swarms that learn the project. 🐝 Stop being middleware: Let WorkerBees escalate to a SmartBee coordinator. You should only see the genuinely new problems. 🐝 Scale without babysitting: One Swarm of agents helped migrate more than 2,000 apps and projects at Block. 🐝 Give teams room to work: Use one or two agents for short tasks. Build a Swarm when the work will run for hours or repeat over days. 🐝 Come back to more finished work: On our long-horizon benchmark, a SmartBee with two WorkerBees team can complete 33% more work . 🐝 Save your expensive frontier tokens: Run QuickBees and WorkerBees at high effort. Spend SmartBee tokens on coordination, judgment, and the hardest decisions. Stop babysitting AI. Build a team that can handle more. Buzz makes it intuitive to use the right model for the right job. Build Hives that learn you & Swarms that learn the project Buzz agents have a name, a persona, a memory that says how it works, and its own presence in the channel. You talk to it the way you talk to a person - by name with the rest of the team. That might sound cosmetic. It is not. Your agents are unique in Buzz with their own memory and persona. The second time it reviews your peer's code it knows which nits you wave off. The tenth time, briefing it is faster than briefing a person. Once an agent is a seat rather than a session, two team shapes naturally show up, and they are good at different things. Hive: A long-term team that knows how you work Make a standing team with a few named agents. Each agent has a job and accumulates memories of your preferences. Customize them to your liking. You talk to each one directly, and each one remembers a different slice of how you work. Swarm: A temporary team, built for one project The other shape is disposable. A migration, a framework bump across every service, a big refactor - work with a start and an end, where the thing worth remembering is the project rather than you. You create the team, let them accumulate a shared memory of the project's edge cases, and delete the team when the work is done. One effective pattern is one SmartBee coordinating a pool of cheap workers, with escalation running back up the chain rather than out to a human. One coordinator, many workers, escalation that stops before it reaches you. Only genuinely new edge cases make it to you. The Swarm gets cheaper to supervise over time because the SmartBee Coordinator handles repeat escalation and saves human answers to memory. I migrated over 2000 apps/projects using Buzz and a Swarm of agents. I created a Swarm with a Coordinator, 1–10 Parallel Migrator Workers, and an Independent Verifier. My Coordinator agent handles the majority of escalations, while I step in to help with new edge cases or clarifications. The agents then learn/remember this for next time. Each migration they get smarter and make less mistakes. - Leigh Maddock, Engineer @ Block Note: Hive and Swarm are blog-specific terms we coined to explain these concepts. Teams come in different shapes and sizes for different needs. Pick the best Bee for the job Not every task needs the same level of intelligence. Reading a stack trace and re-running a build is not the same job as designing a migration across two thousand repositories. Paying frontier prices for the first one is how you end up explaining a inference bill in a meeting you did not want to attend. So let's sort agents into different tier bees! 🐝 The tier + recommended effort helps you remove the noisy model releases. QuickBee Fast and Cheap. Good for documented legwork: builds, screenshots, running the test suite, first-pass triage, etc. GPT-5.6 Luna · DeepSeek V4 Flash · or local models Run at max or xhigh or high effort WorkerBee The all rounder tier. Enough judgement to own a whole subtask end to end without a babysitter, at a fraction of frontier cost. GPT-5.6 Terra · Gemini 3.6 Flash · or open models Run at high or xhigh effort SmartBee Holds the big picture, makes the calls, absorbs the escalations. Pair it with a QuickBee or WorkerBee so it is not burning frontier tokens on legwork. Claude Opus 5 · Kimi K3 · GPT-5.6 Sol Run at medium effort Human honorary bee The most expensive bee on the team, and the slowest. Also still the smartest. Spend it on the escalations nobody else can resolve. You Run at whatever effort you have left 😂 The models are not owned by Block. OpenAI(GPT-5.6 Luna, Sol and Terra), Anthropic(Claude Opus 5), Google(Gemini 3.6 Flash), DeepSeek(DeepSeek V4 Flash), Moonshot AI(Kimi K3) The effort recommendations are not vibes. Here is the same benchmark, one seat, no teammates, across the tiers. Paying more stops helping, then starts hurting. Terminal-Bench 2.1 · one solo agent 5.5× the price spread across the six similar top scorers 8.9 pts the score spread across those same six Run on Harbor , driving real Buzz agents over a live relay. One attempt per task, no retries and with timeouts. * Opus 5 xhigh effort hit the wall clock timeout on 17 of its 88 tasks so has a lower score. ** Kimi K3 and DeepSeek V4 Flash do not support medium effort. Results vary by task, configuration, and environment; prices as of 2026-07-30. Model names are the property of their respective owners and are not owned by Block. Read the two Luna rows first. Turning Luna up from medium to high effort moves to usable while being cheaper. For QuickBees, the advice is "run it hot and high effort": on a cheap model, reasoning tokens are the best deal available. Now read the bottom row. Opus 5 at xhigh effort is the most expensive thing we ran, and it scores worse due to over-reasoning, which resulted in timeouts. Sol does a smaller version of the same thing. SmartBee with Medium effort works well for most tasks. Everything from Terra at medium effort upward is the same agent as far as these tasks can tell. Which is good news, because it means choosing between them is not a quality decision at all. It is a budget decision. Build the best team for the job The amazing thing about Buzz is that agents can call each other!!! A SmartBee can hand a subtask to a WorkerBee, wait, review what came back, and send it around again - without a human relaying anything. The failure mode of agent tooling is not that the work is bad, it is that every ambiguity becomes a notification. When agents can escalate to each other, the SmartBee absorbs the ordinary ones - the flaky test, the ambiguous import, the config that moved - and you only hear about the genuinely new problem. The human stops being middleware and goes back to being the last reviewer. So we benchmarked teams too, and the first answer was not the one we were hoping for. On Terminal-Bench 2.1 we ran twelve team compositions - pairs, triads, cheap swarms under a frontier lead - against the solo agent each one was built around. None of them came out ahead of a solo SmartBee for the price. This makes sense once you realize small tasks that finish in minutes don't have enough structure to divide. More agents mostly buys you the cost of explaining it twice for small tasks. Long-horizon work is a different animal. So we ran the same teams on Long-Horizon Terminal-Bench , where a single task is hours of work, and there is real ground for a team of agents to stand on. On long tasks, the team gets more done. A team of agents is more effective at working longer to finish. +12.4 pts mean reward, and 11.4 of those points are the extra completions 20 vs 15 tasks finished outright, out of 44 - team against solo Also run on Harbor driving real Buzz agents over a live relay against LHTB tasks . See the LHTB snapshot to compare with other solo models. Results vary by task, configuration, and environment; prices as of 2026-07-30. Model names are the property of their respective owners and are not owned by Block. * LHTB was run at 3x the timeout - including solo - since coordination adds overhead.
